#UMich University of Michigan consumer sentiment moves to 51.5 in the final November read (preliminary 51.0; October 48.0), the highest since August, as the midterms lifted expectations and inflation expectations plunged.

▪️ Expectations were revised up to 52.9, the highest since July, but current conditions were revised down to 49.4.
▪️ Per survey director Joanne Hsu, expectations “surged for independents” (up 10.7 points) and rose for Democrats (up 7.1), but fell 11.6 points for Republicans to the lowest since October 2024, the biggest election-month swing in party data covering midterms back to 2006.
▪️ Year-ahead inflation expectations “plunged” to 3.7% from 4.7%, the lowest since February and the biggest one-month drop since June 2025, as gas prices fell.
▪️ Long-run expectations fell to 3.3%, tying June through August for the lowest since March.
▪️ Sentiment still “remains subdued at 9% below February,” before the Iran conflict, and is below every reading before 2022.

BofA’s Hartnett asks “when will rate hikes end?” He says it depends on the Fed:

▪ If the Fed is still Wall Street’s “BFF,” a credit and stock slump will short-circuit the hike cycle. His triggers are investment-grade CDX spreads above 80bp and the S&P 500 below 6,845, wiping out this year’s gain. The S&P closed Thursday at 7,176, 4.8% above that line.
▪ If the Fed is now an inflation “tough guy," the March 18 or April 28 FOMC is the earliest markets can position for “peak rates,” and hard-landing risks grow.

His tells that hike fears are over are a top in the US dollar “wrecking ball” and lows in bitcoin, gold and the Kospi, the “1st casualties of hikes.” None has turned yet:

▪ Bitcoin: down 51% from its October 2025 high and at its lowest since July.
▪ Gold: down 33% from its January high and at its lowest since August 2025.
▪ Kospi: down 47% from its June high and at its lowest since January.
▪ Dollar index: 103.9 at Thursday’s close, its highest since April 2025.

tweets.text:
Thursday was a bearish "outside day" for the S&P 500, with a high above Wednesday’s high and a low below Wednesday’s low and closing below Wednesday’s low. 

On their own, those haven’t been much of a warning. Since 1962, the S&P 500 has had 402 outside days that closed below the prior day’s low, and it was higher a month later 64% of the time, with a median gain of 1.3%, slightly better than the 61% and 1.1% for all days.

But, the 15 that also produced the lowest close in at least 100 sessions (Thursday’s was the lowest in 142) were a coin flip a month later, higher just 47% of the time with a median loss of 0.2%. 

That group includes the 2000–2002 and 2008 bear markets, but also December 19, 2018, three sessions before that selloff’s low, and August 12, 1982, the final low of that bear market. 

But add in that we went from a gain of 1% or more to a loss of 2% or more, and such an outside day has happened just twice before since 1962 (April 19, 1999, and June 28, 2022), with the index higher a month later both times (+3.4% and +6.6%). That's just two cases, though, and in 2022 the index was 4.6% lower three months later, on its way to that year's October low.

MarketWatch flagged a notable shift Thursday: more stocks are starting to fall together (correlations increasing), meaning investors are cutting equity risk across the board, not just selling AI to buy something else. Here’s what the gauge is showing, and how the S&P 500 has performed after similar jumps.

The Cboe 3-Month Implied Correlation Index (COR3M) measures how much the S&P 500’s largest stocks are expected to move together over the next three months. It jumped 24.5% Thursday to 25.34, its highest close since April 1, when the U.S.-Iran war was driving markets. It has now risen six straight days and is up 115% over that stretch.

That’s the biggest six-day rise since the August 2024 yen carry trade unwind (+148%), and bigger than the 103% during the “Liberation Day” panic in April 2025. In Cboe’s data back to 2006, only “Volmageddon” in February 2018 (+172%) and the yen carry unwind were clearly bigger. Covid in February 2020 (+116%) was only slightly bigger.

For context, 25 is still low historically. It sits in the bottom fifth of all readings since 2006, and the 2006–2019 average was about 47. But correlation has run much lower since 2023, and against that period Thursday’s reading is in the top fifth.

Thursday’s jump is a change in character. Cboe’s Mandy Xu noted November 9 that the 1-month version of the index (COR1M) rose only to a “high” of 22% after a 4% one-day S&P drop, when selloffs that size have historically seen implied correlation average closer to 70%, with options still pricing a rotation trade (AI vs. everything else) and little fear of contagion. COR1M closed Thursday at 30.22, its highest since March 30.

The table below the chart shows how the S&P 500 did 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months and 1 year after each of the four prior surges of 90% or more. It was higher a week, six months and a year later all four times, with an average one-year gain of 20.9%. It was higher a month later three times, but three months later only twice.

Widening to the eight surges of 70% or more since 2006, the S&P beat its typical gain at 1 week, 1 month and 1 year, with a median one-year gain of 17.1% against 13.0% for all days. At 3 and 6 months, the median gains were about normal.

Surges like this tend to come in the “sell everything” phase of a pullback, which has usually been nearer the end than the start.

In US economic data, Friday is another light day with just final November University of Michigan consumer sentiment.

Fed speakers include Fed Governors Waller (welcoming remarks at the College Fed Challenge finals) and Cook (on the US economy in a global context, at the Central Bank of Chile’s annual conference).

ECB President Lagarde and the Bundesbank’s Nagel speak at the European Banking Congress, and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham travels to Brussels for the year’s second EU-UK summit.
